messages.subject: Structural Equation Modelling problems with data stack
parts:
Dear all, 

I would like to run a model with the following formula: 

formula_total <- list(
  transf_stability ~ + sc_pr_mean_slope +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc"),
 
  mean_total ~  sc_pr_mean_slope +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc") ,
 
  transf_stability ~ mean_total +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc") ,
 
  mean_total ~ transf_stability +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc") 
) 

When I try to build the data stack, I get the error message that the names for data and effects cannot be the same. Is there a solution for that problem? 

Data stack: 
StackEst1_total <- inla.stack(
  data = list(
    transf_stability = fin_dat$transf_stability,
    mean_total = fin_dat$mean_total
  ),
  A = list(
    1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, A_point, 1 
  ),
  effects = list(
    transf_stability = fin_dat$transf_stability,
    mean_total = fin_dat$mean_total,
    sc_pr_mean_slope = fin_dat$sc_pr_mean_slope,
    w = s.index,
    Intercept = rep(1, nrow(fin_dat))
  ),
  tag = "Est"
) 

Thanks a lot! 
Ramona

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Structural Equation Modelling problems with data stack
parts:
Hi,

It's not clear what the intent of your model is meant to be; if you
want to run them jointly you need (in the plain inla interface) a
single formula.
The short answer is otherwise to change the names of your response
variables, so that it's clear which ones are used as covariates and
when they're used as response variables.

But the details really depend on what the model you want to implement
is; e.g., is the intent that each response variable should be linked
to the same realisation of a common spatial field component, or that
there should be 4 separate model, each with it's own spatial field?

Or did you want the _estimate_ from one model to be used as the
_input_ of the next one? It's not clear from what you wrote. You'd
need to spell out the model definition without referring to the code
(i.e. preferably in text + maths), in order for anyone to know what
the correct code should look like. It's impossible to to correct the
code without knowing exactly what the intent is.

Finn

parts:
Dear Finn (and all others), 

thanks a lot for this quick response! So the problem lies in my formula. 

Maybe it helps to get some background information. I have sampled a share of points in the field. For each sample point I have data for mean_total, transf_stability and sc_pr_mean_slope. Now I would like to understand how those variables are linked and a simple regression is not enough, as I have two dependent variables that are probably influencing each other. In addition to that I would also like to correct for spatial autocorrelation between sampling points.

All response variables can thus be linked to the same spatial field. The model should contain two dependent variables (mean_total, transf_stability) and one independent variable (sc_pr_mean_slope). In addition to that I would like to get information on the relationship between mean_total and transf_stability (does mean_total affect transf_stability and/or does transf_stability affect mean_total?).

Thus, the following structure should be the base:
Y1 ~ X
Y2 ~ X
Y1 ~ Y2
Y2 ~ Y1

But as you found out, I have problems to formulate the formula and the data stack correctly. Especially when I try to include a spatial autocorrelation term.

Is this clearer now? 

Thanks for your help!
Ramona

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Structural Equation Modelling problems with data stack
parts:
Hi Ramona,

models 1&3 are just two different models for the same observed values,
and not a coherent joint model. Same thing with 2&4.
Models 3 and 4 can _not_ in themselves be used to determine whether Y1
_affects_ Y2 and/or Y2 _affects_ Y1; they will only tell you something
about their association, and running them jointly with each other
and/or models 1&3 doesn't give you any benefits, so just run them
separately if you want them at all.
Causal structure is not something you can infer from this; it only
gives you estimates of the model parameters _given_ a specific model
structure.

So that leaves models 1 and 2, that are linked by involving the same
spatial field, and only differing in the parameters of the observation
model (so allowing them to have different observation noise variance,
but otherwise being identical, unless you allow the coefficient for
the covariate, sc_pr_mean_slope, to be different for the two models,
for example. Is that what you are looking for?

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Structural Equation Modelling problems with data stack
parts:
Hi,

it sounds like they're using self-referential regression models, where
the observations are on both sides of the model definition; this is
not the normal statistical regression setup, except in auto-regressive
models.
Since the model definition there is in a different R interface, I
think you really need to write down the "pure" mathematical definition
of the model, with no "R formula" shortcuts. E.g., a normal regression
model (with additive Gaussian observation noise)
with R formula shorthand
y ~ 1 + x
is really defined mathematically as
y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_x x_i + \epsilon_i
where \epsilon_i are independent N(0, \sigma_e^2) and \beta_1 and
\beta_x are model parameters.

In a self-referential model, you might have something like this:
x_i = \beta_1 y_j + a_i
y_j = \beta_2 x_j + b_j
which can be rewritten as
[-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] [x; y] = [a; b]
and
[x; y] = [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] ^{-1} [a; b]
In this case, the rewrite wasn't really necessary, since all the x and
y values were observed, but in other cases such rewrite may be
necessesary;
the initial formulation can in this cas be implemented by simply
renaming the vectors used on the left hand side (as I mentioned in a
previous reply).

If you can write your desired model on this kind of complete
mathematical form, we'll then be able to tell you how to implement it.

Finn

Finn Lindgren schrieb am Mittwoch, 12. Juli 2023 um 14:36:36 UTC+2:
Hi,

it sounds like they're using self-referential regression models, where
the observations are on both sides of the model definition; this is
not the normal statistical regression setup, except in auto-regressive
models.
Since the model definition there is in a different R interface, I
think you really need to write down the "pure" mathematical definition
of the model, with no "R formula" shortcuts. E.g., a normal regression
model (with additive Gaussian observation noise)
with R formula shorthand
y ~ 1 + x
is really defined mathematically as
y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_x x_i + \epsilon_i
where \epsilon_i are independent N(0, \sigma_e^2) and \beta_1 and
\beta_x are model parameters.

In a self-referential model, you might have something like this:
x_i = \beta_1 y_j + a_i
y_j = \beta_2 x_j + b_j
which can be rewritten as
[-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] [x; y] = [a; b]
and
[x; y] = [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] ^{-1} [a; b]
In this case, the rewrite wasn't really necessary, since all the x and
y values were observed, but in other cases such rewrite may be
necessesary;
the initial formulation can in this cas be implemented by simply
renaming the vectors used on the left hand side (as I mentioned in a
previous reply).

If you can write your desired model on this kind of complete
mathematical form, we'll then be able to tell you how to implement it.

Finn

Finn Lindgren schrieb am Mittwoch, 12. Juli 2023 um 14:03:42 UTC+2:

Hi Ramona,

models 1&3 are just two different models for the same observed values,
and not a coherent joint model. Same thing with 2&4.
Models 3 and 4 can _not_ in themselves be used to determine whether Y1
_affects_ Y2 and/or Y2 _affects_ Y1; they will only tell you something
about their association, and running them jointly with each other
and/or models 1&3 doesn't give you any benefits, so just run them
separately if you want them at all.
Causal structure is not something you can infer from this; it only
gives you estimates of the model parameters _given_ a specific model
structure.

So that leaves models 1 and 2, that are linked by involving the same
spatial field, and only differing in the parameters of the observation
model (so allowing them to have different observation noise variance,
but otherwise being identical, unless you allow the coefficient for
the covariate, sc_pr_mean_slope, to be different for the two models,
for example. Is that what you are looking for?

Finn

Finn Lindgren schrieb am Mittwoch, 12. Juli 2023 um 12:25:48 UTC+2:

Hi,

It's not clear what the intent of your model is meant to be; if you
want to run them jointly you need (in the plain inla interface) a
single formula.
The short answer is otherwise to change the names of your response
variables, so that it's clear which ones are used as covariates and
when they're used as response variables.

But the details really depend on what the model you want to implement
is; e.g., is the intent that each response variable should be linked
to the same realisation of a common spatial field component, or that
there should be 4 separate model, each with it's own spatial field?

Or did you want the _estimate_ from one model to be used as the
_input_ of the next one? It's not clear from what you wrote. You'd
need to spell out the model definition without referring to the code
(i.e. preferably in text + maths), in order for anyone to know what
the correct code should look like. It's impossible to to correct the
code without knowing exactly what the intent is.

Finn
